research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. API and reported event

`javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory` creates trust managers from a source of trust material for secure sockets. The reported event concerns the **`init(KeyStore)` overload**, whose argument is documented as a keystore **or `null`**. The API documentation does not itself prescribe one universal default-store lookup procedure for every provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html?utm_source=openai))

For Oracle’s **SunJSSE PKIX and SunX509** factories, passing a null keystore requests their documented default trust-material lookup. In brief, they look for the configured `javax.net.ssl.trustStore`; if that property is absent, they look for `jssecacerts` and then `cacerts`. If the property names a nonexistent file, Oracle documents creation of a trust manager using an empty keystore. This is provider-specific guidance, not a guarantee about every platform. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))

The finding’s “loading was not observed” language is a **detector observation**, not an API event defined by Oracle. The supplied finding information also attributes a representative `UnsatisfiedConstraint` to the *algorithm* allowlist. The published rule separately requires keystore evidence; it does not contain a literal null-keystore test. The available information does not establish which condition produced this particular report. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl))

Sources:
- API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html
- SunJSSE lookup: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

### 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle documents obtaining a factory for an available algorithm, then initializing it with the overload appropriate to the provider: a `KeyStore` or provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters`. `getTrustManagers()` throws `IllegalStateException` if the factory has not been initialized. Java SE requires support for the standard `PKIX` factory algorithm; additional algorithm names depend on the implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

Oracle’s guide documents both default trust-material lookup and use of an explicitly loaded keystore. It **does not characterize null as inherently incorrect**, nor prescribe a universal remediation solely for passing null. Where an explicit trust source is required, the documented alternative is to initialize with an appropriate loaded keystore, or with provider-supported parameters. The appropriate trust material and provider remain deployment requirements, not facts established by the finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))

Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

### 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted formats:** Changing the factory’s initialization source does not itself specify a keystore format conversion. If a separately persisted keystore is used, its type and provider matter. Oracle says the JDK default changed from JKS to PKCS12 in JDK 9, and documents `keytool -importkeystore` as a migration mechanism for JKS or JCEKS stores to PKCS12. That format migration is **not a prerequisite established by this finding**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))
- **Wire formats:** The cited API and guide do not describe a wire-format migration caused merely by changing the keystore argument. Changing trust material can nevertheless change certificate-validation outcomes; the sources do not establish compatibility for a particular peer or certificate set. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Platform support:** Oracle marks the Java SE class as available since Java 1.4. Android documents the class and its two `init` overloads from API level 1. Algorithm and provider availability still need to be checked for the target platform; Java SE’s PKIX requirement should not be assumed to establish support for every named algorithm on Android. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Artifact/version:** The reported class is a platform API. No project declaration, resolved runtime version, or target migration version was supplied, so this research cannot map the finding to a specific project artifact or establish a version-change path.

Sources:
- Keystore formats and migration: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
- Android API: https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory

### 4. Published CrySL rule

The supplied file declares `SPEC javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory`. Its matching event declarations and algorithm constraint are, verbatim:

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
i1: init(keyStore);
i2: init(params);
gtm1: trustManager = getTrustManagers();
```

```text
algorithm in {"PKIX", "SunX509"};
```

The file declares `algorithm` as `String`, `keyStore` as `KeyStore`, and `params` as `ManagerFactoryParameters`. Thus its event declarations specify one- and two-argument `getInstance` forms, the two single-argument `init` forms, and a zero-argument `getTrustManagers` form; the second `getInstance` argument is written `_`. The order is `Get, Init, GetTrustMng?`. The rule separately lists `generatedKeyStore[keyStore]` and `generatedManagerFactoryParameters[params]` under `REQUIRES`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl))

**Namesake methods:** No—the rule is declared for `javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory`; it is not written as a free-standing name-only rule for unrelated receiver types. The file itself does not specify a detector implementation’s resolution, subclass, alias, or unknown-value handling. Nor does it state that the supplied SHA-256 or the detector’s compiled rule corresponds to the current `master` file. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl))
